newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia landslide survivor tells of fight for life.
newsitem.headline: Australia landslide survivor tells of fight for life.

text.p: Ski instructor Stuart Diver, pulled alive from the rubble of a three-day-old Australian landslide, has told rescuers how he fought in vain to save his wife from drowning inside their concrete tomb.
As underground water filled the cavity in which Diver and his wife, Sally, were trapped, the fit ski instructor tried desperately to hold his wife's head above water.

But Sally was pinned on a mattress beside him by something heavy and a sudden rush of water and mud ripped her from Diver's grip. "He hung on desperately, he doesn't know how long for," said rescue helicopter spokesman Bruce Tarrant.

For the next 60-odd hours that Diver remained trapped under tonnes of twisted rubble, he lay on his back, constantly pressing his nose against the concrete slab above his head to breath, as water and mud flooded his tomb.

"A number of times he could hear the rush of water starting to build up behind him and he just knew that he was going to get hit with water again," Paul Featherstone, the paramedic who spent 11 hours underground with Diver, said on Sunday.
"He only had an inch or two inches above his nose and what he would do is he would lift his head and put it against the slab above his head and suck in the air," Featherstone said.
Speaking for the first time from his hospital bed in Canberra, Diver thanked emergency crews for their efforts and all the people who offered prayers for him over the past four days.

"I'd just like to thank everyone who was involved in my rescue, the fire brigade, and all the rescue services along with the medical teams at Thredbo and here in Canberra and all the people who prayed for me and gave me so much support over the last couple of days," the 27-year-old said.
"It's been overwhelming and I don't think I'd have made it through without the involvement of all those people. It's been fantastic, and thanks very much."
Propped up on pillows, Diver looked well despite his ordeal.
What appeared to be an oxygen tube was attached to his nose and a cage surrounded the lower half of his legs.
Doctors described his recovery as miraculous, while rescuers told of how Diver had believed he was going to drown in the "mini-tomb" created by two concrete slabs.
Diver had been entombed between the slabs with only 30 cm (12 inches) in which to move his head and 40 to 50 cm (15 to 19 inches) to move his feet.
"By the time he was rescued there was very little water in there -- he was actually lying in mud," police superintendent Charlie Sanderson said.
"But early in the peace, that site had significant quantities of water flowing through it and he said that for a considerable period of time...he almost drowned."
Diver, who was in bed with his wife when the landslide hit, told rescuers he heard a loud explosion before the two Thredbo Alpine Village ski lodges crumbled, burying 20 people.
"He said it was like a loud explosion. He thought actually that the house had been bombed and that within seconds the whole place erupted," Featherstone said.
When rescuers on Saturday afternoon reached Diver, who had been in complete darkness for almost three days, they found he had no idea of how long he had been trapped.

"He said at times he thought that maybe he just wouldn't get out, but this guy wouldn't let that beat him," said Featherstone, who described the perfect alpine weather outside to Diver to keep his spirits up.
"I kept promising him this afternoon you'll be out and we'll have a look at it together," Featherstone said.
Diver told Featherstone that he travelled the world in his mind, putting himself in places which he had enjoyed in the past, in order to pass the time while rescuers dug him out.
"When he first saw the light, the sky, he just looked at me and he said 'that sky's fantastic'," Featherstone said.
The first doctor to examine Diver, who is now being treated in hospital for hypothermia to one toe and lacerations, described his condition as "remarkable".

"This man's chances of survival were one in a million," Dr Richard Morris said on Sunday. "The fact that he has been able to survive is absolutely remarkable. It's absolutely out of the blue -- it's a miracle."

But while rescuers on Sunday rejoiced in Diver's amazing survival, the search for more survivors and bodies continued in the dangerously shifting landslide site at Thredbo, 400 km (250 miles) south of Sydney.
The number of bodies removed from the wreckage rose to eight on Sunday with police believing they had located a ninth.
Ten people are missing.
